sourceLine: your content filter and chatbot work, and the questions parents ask before they trust a safeguard

cards.title: Chatbot Filtering Without the Provider's Help
cards.angle: California SB 243 (effective January 1 2026) puts duties on companion-chatbot operators, with a private remedy for people who suffer injury. The law binds some operators; the protection gap is every chatbot and account a child can reach that it does not cover.
cards.evidence: Your March 2026 filter works at the browser and device level across ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Perplexity and Claude, routes native apps to filtered browser versions, and holds even when a family switches accounts. You explained the feature already; the deeper follow-up is the protection boundary, what happens in native apps, and how the filter keeps pace with changing outputs.

sources.title: California SB 243 compliance requirements for AI companion chatbots

cards.title: Age Verification Laws Do Not Filter Content
cards.angle: Texas's App Store Accountability Act took effect May 28 2026 after a Fifth Circuit stay, with further state laws on their own timelines. These laws move age categories and consent signals between stores and developers; they do not inspect what a child sees inside an app.
cards.evidence: Your position is that screen-time limits and content filtering are different jobs, and your product replaces explicit images inside otherwise allowed pages in milliseconds. A piece that tells parents which job each safeguard actually does is a traffic piece with a multi-year shelf life.

Screen Time Limits vs Content Filtering

cards.title: Replacing Pixels Beats Blocking Pages
cards.angle: Blocking a whole website is blunt when the unwanted material is one image on an otherwise useful page. Selective replacement needs a classifier fast enough that the page still loads normally, and honest numbers on what it gets wrong.
cards.evidence: Your patented SafeSmart filter replaces explicit images with white rectangles in browsers and some apps, decides in milliseconds, and serves 200,000-plus families by your own count. You publish no latency distribution, false-positive rate or statement of where the model runs; the article that does would separate you from every blocklist competitor.
